experiments.detailed_conditions: 0.1 M dG + 0.1 M Tb(NO₃)₃, pH ≈ 8 (NH₄OH), heat 95 °C 20 min → cool 25 °C; 0.1 M dG + 0.1 M Dy(NO₃)₃, pH ≈ 8, same heat-cool protocol
experiments.detailed_results: Transparent hydrogel, green Tb³⁺ emission (λem ≈ 545 nm); G′ ≈ 200 Pa; Transparent hydrogel, weak yellow Dy³⁺ emission; G′ ≈ 180 Pa
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Each Tb³⁺/Dy³⁺ ion forms square-antiprismatic dG₄·Ln³⁺ clusters via O6/N7 and ribose hydroxyls. π–π stacking of guanine bases plus hydrogen-bond ladders extend the clusters into 1 D columns; lateral association yields nanofibrils only a few nm thick. Entanglement of these high-aspect-ratio fibres traps > 95 % water, giving stiff elastic gels. Efficient guanine → Tb³⁺ energy transfer produces bright green luminescence; Dy³⁺ receives less energy, so emission is weaker. Acid, Cu²⁺ or F⁻ break coordination bonds, collapsing the network and quenching light, while neutralisation or EDTA reverses the process, evidencing coordination-driven, reversible gelation.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL Gd in 0.2 M LiCl; heat-cool.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Gd tends to crystallize in the presence of Li⁺ ions. The hydrogen-bonding and base-stacking interactions are insufficient to maintain a disordered hydrogel network, leading the molecules to assemble into ordered crystalline structures.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL Gd in 0.2 M NaCl; heat-cool.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Na⁺ ions favor ordered molecular packing. Due to the relatively limited hydrogen-bonding and stacking capability of Gd, the supramolecular assemblies preferentially crystallize rather than forming a stable gel network.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL Gd in 0.2 M KCl; heat-cool.
experiments.detailed_results: Gd; mgc 0.9 mg/100 µL; T_gel 50 °C; short-lived/least stable.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: K⁺ ions can template guanosine assemblies through cation coordination, stabilizing hydrogen-bonded tetrad structures. However, Gd has weaker hydrogen-bonding and stacking interactions compared with modified derivatives, resulting in a less stable hydrogel that may eventually crystallize.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 36 mM dG + 18 mM KB(OH)₄ in water; heat–cool protocol.
experiments.detailed_results: Remains a non-viscous solution; no hydrogel observed.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Without the 2′-OH the ribose cannot form borate diesters, so the covalent cross-linking step is lost. G₄·K⁺ quartets may still form but lack lateral cohesion and do not build a percolating fibre network, preventing gelation.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 0.1 M T + 0.1 M Tb(NO₃)₃, pH ≈ 8, 95 °C 20 min → 25 °C; 0.1 M T + 0.1 M Eu(NO₃)₃, pH ≈ 8, heat–cool
experiments.detailed_results: Transparent hydrogel, green Tb³⁺ luminescence; G′ ≈ 20 Pa (softer); Transparent hydrogel, red Eu³⁺ luminescence; G′ ≈ 20 Pa
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Thymine carbonyl and ring-nitrogen sites coordinate Tb³⁺/Eu³⁺ in 3:1 T₃·Ln³⁺ complexes. Complexes stack through π–π overlap of the thymine rings, while ribose OH⋯O=C hydrogen bonds laterally bundle the fibres into thicker tapes than in dG gels, accounting for the lower modulus. Metal-ligand bonds remain dynamic: heating, pH swing or Cu²⁺ compete with Ln³⁺, causing reversible luminescence quenching and gel–sol transitions. Thus gelation stems from cooperative metal coordination, base stacking and sugar-hydrogen bonding, with bundle thickness modulating mechanical softness.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 0.1 M U + 0.1 M Tb(NO₃)₃, pH ≈ 8, 95 °C 20 min → 25 °C; 0.1 M U + 0.1 M Eu(NO₃)₃, pH ≈ 8, heat–cool
experiments.detailed_results: Green-emissive hydrogel (Tb³⁺), fibre bundles, elastic network; Red-emissive hydrogel (Eu³⁺), morphology, stiffness similar to T gels.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Uracil carbonyl pairs and N3 coordinate Ln³⁺ to give U₃·Ln³⁺ complexes that π–π stack and cross-link through extensive ribose hydroxyl hydrogen bonds, forming bundled fibres. Compared with dG, the 3:1 stoichiometry and lower base-stacking energy yield thicker fibres and smaller G′. Lanthanide-centered emission is sensitised by uracil singlet–triplet transitions; coordination disruption by pH or competing anions dims the emission and liquefies the gel, highlighting the key role of reversible metal–ligand and hydrogen-bond interactions.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 50 mM U with 25 mM B(OH)₃ and 25 mM AgNO₃, pH basic, room temperature.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Uridine can form borate diesters but lacks the cytosine base needed for Ag⁺-mediated C·Ag⁺·C pairing; without metal-stabilised base dimers the network does not nucleate, so gelation fails despite the presence of borate cross-links.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL isoG in 0.2 M LiCl; dissolve at ≈80 °C, then cool to room temperature (pH 3–10, incl. PBS).
experiments.detailed_results: Stable transparent hydrogels; G′ about 15 × higher than guanosine gels; lifetime up to 3 months.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: isoG self-assembles into isoG quartets or pentaplexes stabilized by hydrogen bonding and Li⁺ coordination. These assemblies stack into helical fibers that interconnect into a robust three-dimensional network, producing a stable hydrogel

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL isoG in 0.2 M NaCl; dissolve at ≈80 °C, then cool to room temperature (pH 3–10, incl. PBS).
experiments.detailed_results: Stable transparent hydrogels; G′ about 15 × higher than guanosine gels; lifetime up to 3 months.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Na⁺ ions coordinate with isoG assemblies, stabilizing hydrogen-bonded isoG quartets or pentaplexes. These supramolecular units stack into interconnected helical fibers, creating a stable three-dimensional gel network.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL isoG in 0.2 M KCl; dissolve at ≈80 °C, then cool to room temperature (pH 3–10, incl. PBS).
experiments.detailed_results: Stable transparent hydrogels; G′ about 15 × higher than guanosine gels; lifetime up to 3 months.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: K⁺ ions effectively template isoG quartet or pentaplex assemblies through cation coordination. The stacked assemblies form flexible helical fibers that interconnect into a dense three-dimensional network, giving rise to a stable hydrogel.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL isoGd in 0.2 M LiCl; heat–cool cycle, pH 3–10.
experiments.detailed_results: Forms a transparent and stable hydrogel with a lifetime of approximately two months
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The 2′-deoxy modification increases hydrophobic interactions, promoting self-assembly into isoGd quartets or pentaplexes stabilized by hydrogen bonding and Li⁺ coordination. These assemblies stack into interconnected fiber networks that maintain gel stability.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL isoGd in 0.2 M KCl; heat–cool cycle, pH 3–10.
experiments.detailed_results: Produces long-lived (≥ 3 months) non-fluorescent hydrogels with K⁺.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: K⁺ ions effectively coordinate with isoGd assemblies, stabilizing hydrogen-bonded quartets or pentaplexes. These stacked supramolecular units generate interconnected fibers that form a robust three-dimensional hydrogel network.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL isoGd in 0.2 M NaCl; heat–cool cycle, pH 3–10.
experiments.detailed_results: Does not form a hydrogel; the system remains in solution or forms precipitates.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Na⁺ ions do not effectively stabilize the supramolecular quartet or pentaplex assemblies of isoGd. Without sufficient cation templating, the hydrogen-bonded structures fail to form the interconnected fiber network required for hydrogel formation; meanwhile, their ion selectivity reflects the varying degrees of fit of different cations within the tetrameric cavities.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL FisoGd in 0.2 M LiCl.
experiments.detailed_results: Forms a transparent and stable hydrogel with stability up to about two months.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The fluorine substitution at the 2′ position enhances hydrophobic interactions and strengthens hydrogen bonding. These interactions promote the formation of isoG-like quartets or pentaplexes stabilized by Li⁺ coordination, which stack into interconnected fiber networks forming a hydrogel.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL FisoGd in 0.2 M NaCl.
experiments.detailed_results: Forms a transparent hydrogel that remains stable for up to two months.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Fluorine substitution boosts hydrophobicity and strengthens base stacking while polarising adjacent C–H···F interactions. These effects lower the critical concentration for quartet assembly and reinforce the cation-bridged fibrillar network, preserving the long-term stability seen in isoG systems.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL FisoGd in 0.2 M KCl.
experiments.detailed_results: Forms a transparent and stable hydrogel with a lifetime of approximately two months.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: K⁺ ions effectively stabilize hydrogen-bonded FisoGd quartets or pentaplexes through cation coordination. The fluorine substitution strengthens base stacking and intermolecular interactions, allowing stacked assemblies to form a robust three-dimensional hydrogel network.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL G in 0.2 M LiCl.
experiments.detailed_results: Forms a hydrogel initially, but the gel collapses within minutes and loses structural integrity rapidly.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Guanosine forms G-quartet structures stabilized by hydrogen bonding and Li⁺ coordination, but the resulting assemblies organize into flat ribbon-like structures with weak crosslinking. This limited network connectivity results in very poor mechanical stability and rapid gel collapse.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL G in 0.2 M NaCl.
experiments.detailed_results: Forms a hydrogel initially, but the gel collapses within minutes and quickly disintegrates.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Although Na⁺ ions can participate in stabilizing G-quartet assemblies, the supramolecular structures formed by guanosine tend to organize into discrete ribbon-like aggregates. These structures lack sufficient crosslinking to maintain a stable three-dimensional gel network.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 5 mM KCl + 100 mM NaCl.
experiments.detailed_results: Does not gel at lower, physiologically relevant salt concentrations.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: G-Quartet Dependence: Relies on the formation of G-quartets stabilized by high concentrations of monovalent ions.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL G in 0.2 M KCl.
experiments.detailed_results: Forms a transparent hydrogel, but it disintegrates within approximately 15 hours.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: K⁺ ions more effectively stabilize G-quartet assemblies through cation coordination. However, the resulting flat ribbon-like microstructures produce weakly interconnected networks, leading to limited mechanical strength and eventual gel collapse.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 354 mM KCl.
experiments.detailed_results: G-quartet hydrogel forms at high KCl but crystallises within hours (~≤36 h); gelator 5 mg mL⁻¹; no gel at low salt.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Classical K⁺-stabilised G-quartets stack into ribbons with weak lateral cohesion; water drains and crystals nucleate, giving short-lived gels.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 5 mM KCl.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: G-Quartet Dependence: Relies on the formation of G-quartets stabilized by high concentrations of monovalent ions.

experiments.detailed_conditions: Upon addition of 0.5 equivalents of KCl to a 2 wt% (2.1 mM) aqueous solution. Heat-cool.
experiments.detailed_results: The resulting hydrogel is transient, quickly transforming into a precipitate within approximately 30 minutes.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The primary reason G fails to form a stable hydrogel is its low water solubility (2.1 mM). This insufficient solubility leads to rapid precipitation rather than the formation of a stable, self-standing hydrogel. The imbalance between hydrophobicity and hydrophilicity prevents the stable assembly of G4·K⁺ quartets necessary for hydrogel formation, favoring instead crystallization or precipitation.

experiments.detailed_conditions: KCl (0.354 M) + TAcG (G:TAcG = 60:40–40:60); heat to dissolution (~100°C) and cool to room temperature.
experiments.detailed_results: Formation of stable, self-supporting hydrogels with dramatically enhanced lifetime stability (no crystallization observed after >1 year at room temperature, compared to hours for G alone); Thermal stability (Tgel-sol) enhanced to >60°C (peak ~63°C for 50/50 ratio vs ~50°C for G alone).
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Co-assembly of G and TAcG into mixed G-quartet stacks. The bulky acetyl groups of TAcG introduce structural heterogeneity that sterically hinders long-range ordering and crystallization (enhancing lifetime stability) and truncates fiber growth (reducing fiber length and mechanical strength at RT). Simultaneously, the hydrophobic acetyl groups provide physical cross-linking via the hydrophobic effect, which enhances thermal stability and contributes to an unusual increase in modulus at elevated temperatures (45-60°C), compensating for the loss of hydrogen bonding and pi-pi interactions.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 36 mM G + 18 mM KB(OH)₄ (0.5 equiv) in water; heated to 90 °C then cooled.
experiments.detailed_results: GB hydrogels made with 0.5 equiv KB(OH)₄ have remained transparent for over a year.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Borate forms diesters with the ribose cis-diol, dimerising guanosine and positioning it for G₄·K⁺ quartet stacking. The borate diesters act as covalent cross-links, while optimally sized K⁺ ions template and stabilise the stacked quartets. π–π stacking plus hydrogen bonding between quartets yields long nanofibres that entangle into a highly stable network; removal of either borate or K⁺ disrupts this dual stabilisation and the gel fails.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 36 mM G + KB(OH)₄ (< 0.5 equiv) in water; heated to 90 °C then cooled.
experiments.detailed_results: Insufficient borate; incomplete nucleoside dissolution; no stable network.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Less than 0.5 equiv leads to incomplete dissolution of guanosine. Deviations from this ratio disrupt the balance between monoester and diester formation, undermining gel stability.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 36 mM G + 18 mM LiB(OH)₄ (0.5 equiv) in water; heated to 90 °C then cooled.
experiments.detailed_results: Formation of a free-flowing solution. No gelation or fibril formation observed.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Although LiB(OH)₄ helps dissolve the substrate by forming borate esters (as noted in other parts of the text), the Li+ cation is unable to stabilize the G-quartet (G₄) structure effectively compared to K⁺. Without the stable G₄ core templated by the cation, the supramolecular assembly into nanowires and gel does not occur.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL z8isoGd in 0.2 M LiCl, dissolve at > 90 °C, then cool to room-temperature
experiments.detailed_results: Does not form a hydrogel; precipitation or solution state is observed.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Li⁺ ions cannot effectively template the supramolecular assemblies required for z8isoGd gelation. Without suitable cation coordination, the hydrogen-bonded pentad or tetrad stacking necessary for fiber network formation cannot be stabilized.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL z8isoGd in 0.2 M NaCl, dissolve at > 90 °C, then cool to room-temperature
experiments.detailed_results: Does not form a hydrogel; precipitation or solution state is observed.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Na⁺ ions do not provide the optimal ionic radius or coordination environment needed to stabilize the supramolecular assemblies of z8isoGd. As a result, the stacked pentad or tetrad structures required for hydrogel network formation do not develop.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL z8isoGd in 0.2 M KCl, dissolve at > 90 °C, then cool to room-temperature
experiments.detailed_results: Forms a stable and transparent fluorescent hydrogel with a high gel melting temperature (T_gel ≈ 77 °C) ; minimum-gelation-concentration 0.3 mg / 100 µL; lifetime > 3 months; reversible gel ⇄ sol under heating or 366 nm UV.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The 8-azapurine core lowers N⁷ basicity, favouring pentad/tetrad assemblies in which K⁺ is ideally sized to bridge the carbonyl O6 centres. These K-templated disks π-stack and bundle into dense nanofibrils observed by SEM. Extensive H-bond ladders along the sugar rims lock the bundles, giving high T_gel and long-term stability, while efficient base-to-Ln energy transfer renders the network intrinsically fluorescent and thermo-responsive.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL z8isoGd in 0.005 M KCl, dissolve at > 90 °C, then cool to room-temperature
experiments.detailed_results: Gels can form at lower KCl concentrations down to 0.005 M, suitable for biological and medical applications.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The selective formation of hydrogels in the presence of K⁺ ions is hypothesized to stem from the ion's optimal size and charge density, which template the assembly of pentadecameric or tetradecameric structures.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL z8Gd in H₂O with 0.2 M LiCl; heat-cool cycle.
experiments.detailed_results: Remains sol/does not gel on cooling after dissolution.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Replacing N8 with nitrogen diminishes N⁷ basicity, disrupting Hoogsteen hydrogen-bonding required for quartet stacking in water. In the solid state, water is removed and z8Gd can form tetrad columns that curl into nanotubes, but in aqueous media hydrogen-bond competition prevents the cross-linked network necessary for gelation.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.4 mg / 100 µL z8Gd in H₂O with 0.2 M KCl; heat-cool cycle.
experiments.detailed_results: Does not form hydrogels in aqueous solutions of alkali metal ions.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Replacing N8 with nitrogen diminishes N⁷ basicity, disrupting Hoogsteen hydrogen-bonding required for quartet stacking in water. In the solid state, water is removed and z8Gd can form tetrad columns that curl into nanotubes, but in aqueous media hydrogen-bond competition prevents the cross-linked network necessary for gelation.

experiments.detailed_results: Does not form hydrogels in aqueous solutions of alkali metal ions.

In the solid state, water is removed and z8Gd can form tetrad columns that curl into nanotubes, but in aqueous media hydrogen-bond competition prevents the cross-linked network necessary for gelation.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.7–5.0 wt % in H₂O; heat to dissolve, then cool to 25 °C.
experiments.detailed_results: Forms a robust and transparent hydrogel at 25 °C, withstands ≥38 °C and reforms within seconds after shear; thermo-reversible (Tgel ≈ 77 °C at 5 wt %); storage modulus up to 1 MPa; self-heals and remains intact > 10 months; injectable through syringe needle.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Double NH₂ groups on the 2,6-diaminopurine base form Hoogsteen-type pairs, while the 2′-F participates in strong H···F hydrogen bonds. Water molecules bridge adjacent base pairs, generating an extended, ‘water-reinforced’ H-bond network. Together with π–π stacking of purine rings, these interactions produce tightly packed fibrous bundles whose dense cross-links give the gel its exceptionally high modulus, longevity and rapid self-healing behaviour.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.7–5.0 wt % in PBS; heat to dissolve, then cool to 25 °C.
experiments.detailed_results: Switching from water to PBS does not disrupt the supramolecular structure; gels stable above 38 °C.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Double NH₂ groups on the 2,6-diaminopurine base form Hoogsteen-type pairs, while the 2′-F participates in strong H···F hydrogen bonds. Water molecules bridge adjacent base pairs, generating an extended, ‘water-reinforced’ H-bond network. Together with π–π stacking of purine rings, these interactions produce tightly packed fibrous bundles whose dense cross-links give the gel its exceptionally high modulus, longevity and rapid self-healing behaviour.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.7–5.0 wt % in H₂O or PBS, heat–cool protocol.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: 2′-OH makes molecules tend to form more intramolecular hydrogen bonds (such as O2′-H2′···O3′), leaving no extra hydrogen donor to bring water molecules into the hydrophilic regions. The weaker stacking combined with excessive solvation of the ribose prevents formation of the bound-water-reinforced fibrous network.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 1.7–5.0 wt % in H₂O or PBS, thermal treatment.
experiments.detailed_results: Remains a clear solution; no macroscopic gel observed.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Although bases can form hogustin pairs, hydrogen bonds are not sufficient. The sugar therefore stays highly hydrated and the stacked fibres fail to cross-link into a space-filling network, preventing gelation under the tested conditions.

experiments.detailed_conditions: Pure H₂O, heat until dissolved, then cool to room-temperature.
experiments.detailed_results: White opaque, mechanically stable hydrogel; minimum-gelation-concentration (MGC) 0.3 wt %.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The benzyl-triazole ring adds hydrophobic surface and an aromatic π-system that stacks in parallel columns, while the native uridine base and 3′/5′-OH groups supply a hydrogen-bond lattice. Cooperative π–π stacking and H-bonding create fibrous aggregates that interweave into a solvent-filled network; the moderate hydrophobicity of the para-free benzyl substituent gives sufficient packing without excessive steric hindrance, yielding a stable gel.

experiments.detailed_conditions: Water, acidic pH (≤ 2); 0.5–1 wt % heated to dissolve then cooled to rt.
experiments.detailed_results: Gel used as template for TEOS sol-gel polymerisation under the same acidic conditions. At acidic pH forms a clear hydrogel composed of linear fibres 0.7–2 µm wide and several µm long; gel remains stable for hours and withstands silica transcription.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Protonation of the triazole nitrogens under acidic conditions introduces cationic sites that electrostatically attract the anionic oligomeric silica species generated from TEOS. These interactions, together with residual amide N–H···O hydrogen bonds, anchor silica onto the gel fibres while stabilising the supramolecular network. When the medium is neutralised, protonation is lost, electrostatic binding ceases and the fibre scaffold collapses, explaining the pH-sensitive gel–sol behaviour and the requirement for acid in producing porous silica replicas.

experiments.detailed_conditions: Introducing a small amount of benzyl amine (a base).
experiments.detailed_results: Immediate disappearance of the gel upon base addition; demonstrates strong pH sensitivity (protonation of triazole is required).
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The addition of a base (benzyl amine) disrupts protonation, leading to gel destabilization and cessation of effective silica transcription.

experiments.detailed_conditions: Pure H₂O, heat–cool procedure; 0.2 wt% to 3 wt%.
experiments.detailed_results: Unstable white opaque gel (UG) at 3 wt %; collapses on slight agitation.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The ortho-methyl group pushes the aromatic ring out of register, weakening π–π stacking and introducing steric clashes that interrupt fibre growth. The diminished anisotropic aggregation cannot lock enough solvent, so only a fragile, metastable network forms.

experiments.detailed_conditions: Pure H₂O, heat–cool; 0.2 wt% to 3 wt%.
experiments.detailed_results: Unstable white opaque gel (UG) at 1 wt %.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Meta-methyl substitution perturbs planarity less than ortho but still offsets aromatic overlap; fibre bundles are thinner and cross-link sparsely, giving a weak network susceptible to collapse.

experiments.detailed_conditions: Pure H₂O, heat until clear, cool; 0.2 wt% to 3 wt%.
experiments.detailed_results: White opaque, stable hydrogel; MGC 0.6 wt %.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: A para-methyl group maintains planar benzyl orientation, allowing efficient π stacking of the triazole–benzyl chromophores. Together with uridine-based H-bond columns, this drives densely entangled fibrous assemblies that trap water and afford a stable gel, albeit at a slightly higher concentration than the ethyl analogue.

experiments.detailed_conditions: Pure H₂O, heat–cool; 0.2 wt% to 3 wt%.
experiments.detailed_results: Unstable white opaque gel (UG) at 2 wt %.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The ortho-ethyl chain is bulkier than methyl, amplifying steric hindrance and disrupting π–π column formation; hydrophobic mismatch encourages phase separation rather than uniform fibre entanglement, so only a loose, short-lived gel transiently appears.

experiments.detailed_conditions: Pure H₂O, dissolve on heating, cool to room temperature; 0.2 wt% to 3 wt%.
experiments.detailed_results: White opaque, highly stable hydrogel; MGC 0.2 wt %; fibrous network by SEM; retains gel state under inversion and mild shaking.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The para-ethyl substituent adds just enough hydrophobic character to balance the highly hydrophilic deoxyuridine scaffold without introducing steric frustration. π–π stacking among benzyl-triazole rings aligns with an extensive hydrogen-bond grid between nucleobase carbonyls and sugar OH groups. This dual interaction scheme yields densely entangled fibres with large internal voids that absorb solvent, explaining the exceptionally low MGC and superior mechanical/thermal stability of this compound.

experiments.detailed_conditions: Pure H₂O, heat–cool; 0.8 wt% to 3 wt%.
experiments.detailed_results: White opaque, stable hydrogel; MGC 0.8 wt %.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The longer para-butyl chain enhances hydrophobic aggregation and π-stacking but begins to segregate, so fibre packing remains effective yet less optimal than the ethyl analogue. The resulting network still benefits from hydrogen-bond cross-links, yielding a stable gel.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 0.5 wt % in ethanol / water (ΦEtOH ≈ 0.05); dissolve at 60 °C, add pre-heated water, cool to rt 18 h.
experiments.detailed_results: Most robust gelator of the gemcitabine series; stands inversion, shows moderately cross-linked nanofibres (1–40 nm Ø, hundreds µm long); G′ ≫ G″ at 37 °C (tan δ ≈ 0.2–0.3).
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The 4-amide adds a medium-length alkyl chain that supplies hydrophobic surface yet leaves the gemcitabine core fully H-bond competent. Cooperative N-amide···O=C and base-to-base hydrogen bonding align the molecules, while π-stacking between pyrimidine rings nucleates one-dimensional columns. Solvophobic collapse in the ethanol-rich mixture drives lateral association of these columns into an entangled, fibrous network; the hydrophobic tails pack inside, shielding the fibres from water and stabilising the gel.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 0.5 wt % in ethanol / water (ΦEtOH ≈ 0.05); 60 °C dissolution, cool to rt 18 h.
experiments.detailed_results: Most stable gelator of the lamivudine set; forms loose but continuous fibre network; withstands inversion; viscoelastic solid-like response.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The octanoyl chain balances the highly polar oxathiolane ring, optimising solvophobic collapse upon cooling. Amide NH and carbonyl O engage in inter-strand hydrogen bonding, while π–π stacking among the cytidine-like bases propagates columnar growth. Cross-link points arise where oxathiolane OH groups bridge adjacent fibres, giving a softer yet stable gel that survives handling.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 0.5 wt % in ethanol / water; 60 °C dissolution → cool.
experiments.detailed_results: Did not yield a self-supporting gel (solution flows on inversion).
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The long 5′-ester chain makes the molecule too bulky for close base stacking and buries hydrogen-bond donors, so solvophobic aggregation produces amorphous clusters rather than ordered fibres, preventing gelation.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 0.5 wt % in ethanol/water (anti-solvent method, ΦEtOH varied), dissolve at 60 °C in EtOH then add 60 °C water, cool to r.t. 18 h, vial-inversion test
experiments.detailed_results: Did not form a stable gel under screening conditions; sample flowed on inversion
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The long dodecanoyl chain increases hydrophobic bulk around the 5′-ester, causing steric hindrance that frustrates π-stacking and intermolecular H-bond alignment of the gemcitabine cores; molecules therefore aggregate into amorphous clusters rather than an extended fibrous network.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 0.5 wt % in ethanol/water (anti-solvent method, ΦEtOH varied), dissolve at 60 °C in EtOH then add 60 °C water, cool to r.t. 18 h, vial-inversion test
experiments.detailed_results: No self-supporting gel observed; solution remained liquid after 18 h
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The short hexanoyl chain provides insufficient hydrophobic driving force for solvophobic collapse, while the 5′-ester blocks potential hydrogen-bond donors at the ribose; lacking cooperative H-bonding and π-stacking, the compound fails to organise into a percolating fibre network.

experiments.detailed_conditions: Water + 0.05 M NaOH: ≤ 0.5 % w/v.
experiments.detailed_results: In NaOH the sample remains insoluble/precipitated.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The dodecanoyl chain is too short to provide the hydrophobic surface needed to offset electrostatic repulsion after partial NaOH hydrolysis, so the Na⁺-bridged lamella cannot percolate in water.

experiments.detailed_conditions: Organic: opaque organogels in CHCl₃ (1.4 % w/v) and benzene (1.3 % w/v) after heat-cool cycle.
experiments.detailed_results: In non-polar solvents forms self-supporting organogels.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: In CHCl₃ the same chain promotes solvophobic collapse, allowing π–π stacked ribothymine columns and fatty-chain interdigitation to yield a fibrous organogel network.

experiments.detailed_conditions: Studied alone (≤ 2 wt %); heat-to-100 °C then cool protocol.
experiments.detailed_results: TAcG alone is a nongelator. In G/TAcG mixtures (40–60 % TAcG) the hydrogels stay transparent and crystalline-free > 1 year, with storage modulus and yield stress decreasing as TAcG fraction rises.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Acetyl groups sterically cap guanosine stacks and introduce hydrophobic cross-links. When co-assembled with G, TAcG disrupts the regular G₄ stacking that drives crystallisation, yielding shorter but thicker fibres. Hydrophobic acetyl contacts act as additional, temperature-resistant cross-links, raising gel-to-sol transition temperature (~63 °C for 50 / 50 mix) and preventing crystal growth. Increasing TAcG therefore tunes mechanical softness while dramatically extending gel lifetime.

experiments.detailed_conditions: Dissolved at 60–90 °C in 0.5 M acetate buffer (pH 6.0) containing 15–90 mM K⁺, then cooled to room temperature.
experiments.detailed_results: Gelation observed at 10–50 mM. K⁺ is the most effective ion (Tgel ≈ 33 °C at 10 mM, rising to 65 °C at 50 mM; plateaus at KCl ≥ 45 mM). No gel at pH ≥ 8.0; free-standing, transparent hydrogel that withstands vial-inversion for several days; thermoreversible (melts on heating, reforms on cooling); fibres several µm long seen by TEM.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Self-associates through Hoogsteen hydrogen-bonding into G-quartets that stack into K⁺-bridged columns; the hydrazide substituent stabilises the quartet edges and increases π-stacking efficiency, yielding thicker, entangled nanofibrils.  Potassium, being size-matched to the G₄ cavity, maximally stabilises the columnar array.

experiments.detailed_conditions: Acetate buffer (pH 6.0) + Na⁺.
experiments.detailed_results: Gels form with lower efficiency vs K⁺; thermoreversible.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Na⁺ can stabilize G-quartet assemblies formed by guanosine hydrazide through coordination within the central channel of stacked G-quartets, enabling supramolecular fiber formation. However, Na⁺ fits less optimally than K⁺ in the G-quartet cavity, resulting in weaker stabilization of the stacked structures and therefore lower gelation efficiency.

experiments.detailed_conditions: Acetate buffer (pH 6.0) + NH₄⁺.
experiments.detailed_results: Gels form with lower efficiency vs K⁺; thermoreversible.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: NH₄⁺ ions, having an ionic radius similar to K⁺, can template the formation of G-quartets which stack into columns, inducing gelation, though less efficiently than K⁺.

experiments.detailed_conditions: Acetate buffer (pH 6.0) + Me₄N⁺.
experiments.detailed_results: Gels form but with the lowest efficiency among the tested cations (Sequence: K⁺ > Me₄N⁺ > NH₄⁺ > Na⁺); thermoreversible.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Despite its larger size, Me₄N⁺ still induces G-quartet formation and stacking leading to gelation, demonstrating that cation templating is not strictly limited to ions fitting perfectly within the quartet center, although efficiency varies significantly with cation nature.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 50 mM C + 25 mM B(OH)₃ + 25 mM AgNO₃ in water (basic, KB(OH)₄ present); room-temperature self-assembly.
experiments.detailed_results: Transparent, self-supporting hydrogel (G′ up to 10⁴ Pa) that remains intact and photostable for > 1 year; thixotropic and printable; Ag⁺ confers broad-spectrum antibacterial activity.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Gelation arises from two orthogonal interactions: (i) dynamic borate-diester cross-links between cis-2′,3′-diol groups on the ribose (C–B–C) provide covalent junctions, and (ii) Ag⁺-mediated C·Ag⁺·C base pairs stack into one-dimensional columns. Hydrogen bonding and electrostatic forces bundle these columns into entangled nanofibres, giving a robust, stimuli-responsive network whose stability and antibacterial function depend critically on Ag⁺ coordination.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 50 mM C + 25 mM B(OH)₃ + 25 mM K⁺/Cu²⁺/Hg²⁺/Zn²⁺ or Mg²⁺; room-temperature self-assembly.
experiments.detailed_results: No gelation observed under otherwise identical conditions.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Only Ag⁺ ions among the tested metal cations (K⁺, Cu²⁺, Hg²⁺, Zn²⁺, Mg²⁺) effectively promoted gelation, highlighting the unique role of Ag⁺ in stabilizing the necessary supramolecular interactions.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 50 mM nucleoside, 25 mM B(OH)₃, 25 mM AgNO₃, pH basic, room temperature.

experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The trans-2′,3′-diol prevents borate-diester formation, so covalent C–B–C cross-links cannot develop.  Without this scaffold the Ag⁺-paired bases fail to organise into a percolating fibre network, eliminating macroscopic gelation.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 50 mM C + 25 mM B(OH)₃ + 25 mM AgNO₃ in water (basic, KB(OH)₄ present); room-temperature self-assembly.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Removal of both 2′ and 3′ hydroxyl groups abolishes vicinal diols, so borate cross-linking is impossible; lacking covalent junctions the Ag⁺-mediated dimers cannot assemble beyond small aggregates.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 36 mM inosine + 18 mM KB(OH)₄.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Although inosine can form borate esters, the absence of the guanine NH₂ group weakens hydrogen bonding within prospective G₄ quartets, so the assemblies cannot grow into stabilised fibres.

experiments.detailed_conditions: 2 equivalents of KB(OH)₄; heat to 90°C and then cool at room temperature.
experiments.detailed_results: When cooled immediately, a transparent, self-supporting hydrogel formed (G' ~700 Pa for 72 mM gel) that appeared stable for weeks at rt. When kept at 90°C for 15 min before cooling, a viscous solution was obtained instead of a gel.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The 2',3'-diol of 5'-IG reacts with borate from KB(OH)₄ to form anionic guanosine-borate (GB) diesters. These esters self-assemble via hydrogen bonds and π-π stacking to form G4-wires, which entangle into a hydrogel network. However, 5'-IG can undergo an intramolecular cyclization where N3 displaces the 5'-iodide leaving group, forming 5'-deoxy-N3,5'-cycloguanosine (5'-cG). This cyclization is facilitated by a syn conformation of the nucleoside and deprotonation of N1H (pKa ~9) at the gel pH (~8.6). The resulting 5'-cG lacks an N1-H hydrogen bond donor, making its hydrogen bonding pattern incompatible with stable G4-quartet formation. Its in situ formation thus disrupts the gel network, leading to 'self-destruction.

experiments.detailed_results: Formed hydrogels that showed much better lifetime stability than D-G gels. For instance, crystals were observed in 2.8% w/v L-G gels only on day 17, whereas D-G gels crystallized within 24 hours.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: The K⁺ ionic radius is optimal to fit into and stabilize the supramolecular structure. The difference in chirality means the anti-conformation is optimal for L-G (compared to syn-conformation for D-G). This distinct spatial configuration produces different fiber arrangements and differences in steric hindrance, resulting in a more stable gel network.

experiments.detailed_conditions: Sodium borate.
experiments.detailed_results: The hydrogel exhibited a more regular and distinct polyporous membrane-like network and demonstrated favorable biocompatibility, making it a suitable candidate for three-dimensional cell culture extracellular matrices.
experiments.mechanistic_explanation: Borates form dynamic covalent borate diester bonds with the ribose ring, which are stronger than standard non-covalent bonds. These diester bonds act as an adhesive agent, bonding the gelators tighter to enhance molecular interactions, propping the structures up, and leading to more compact crosslinking. NOE experiments confirmed that L-G maintains its optimal anti-conformation within this crosslinked network.
